# 1.1 Principles of Economics

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## What economics studies

**Economics** is the study of how society manages scarce resources. The subject exists because of **scarcity** — the limited nature of society's resources. Nothing is available in unlimited quantity, so every use of a resource rules out some other use, and the whole discipline follows from that.

The questions economics mainly asks are of two kinds. Households decide what to buy, how much work to do, and how much to save and how much to spend. At the level of society, the questions are what to produce and how much employment there will be. Both sets of questions come down to the same thing: dividing resources.

## Why economics is a science

Economics is treated as a science because economists work in the way scientists do. They collect data. They use theories to explain the phenomena in that data. They analyse the **natural experiments** offered by history — episodes the world has already run, which economists cannot stage for themselves. And they follow the **scientific method**: the testing of theories against observations.

## Microeconomics and macroeconomics

The subject splits into two halves according to the scale of the decision being studied.

| | Microeconomics | Macroeconomics |
|---|---|---|
| What it studies | How households and firms make decisions | Economy-wide phenomena — how a nation makes decisions |
| Examples | What to buy, how much to produce | Inflation, unemployment, growth |

## Positive and normative statements

A second division runs through everything an economist says, and it is about the kind of claim being made rather than its scale.

| | Positive statements | Normative statements |
|---|---|---|
| What kind of claim | Descriptive statement (fact) | Prescriptive statement (opinion) |
| Example | "The price is rising"; "Price will rise in 5 years" | (the guide gives none) |

A positive statement describes the world and can in principle be checked against it. A normative statement prescribes, and rests on a judgement rather than on a fact. The guide prints "Price will rise in 5 years" in the normative column; that is an error — a forecast still describes what will happen rather than what ought to happen, so it is positive.

## The four principles of economy

**1. People face trade-offs.** Getting one thing usually means giving up another; the guide's example of such a pairing is efficiency against equality. The guide prints this trade-off as "Efficiency vs Quality"; that is an error — efficiency against equality (equity) is the pairing meant.

**2. The cost of something is what you give up.** This is **opportunity cost**: the second best alternative given up. It is the second best alternative, not the sum of everything forgone — only one alternative would actually have been taken.

**3. Rational people think at the margin.** Rational people systematically do the best they can to profit, and they do it by comparing **marginal benefit** against **marginal cost** — the benefit and the cost of one more unit of whatever is being decided, rather than of the whole activity.

**4. People respond to incentives.** An **incentive** is something that induces a person to act. Incentives come in two forms, award and punishment, and both work by changing the marginal benefit or the marginal cost of an action.

## Worked example: command economies and capitalist economies

*Command economies differ from capitalist economies mainly because of which of the following?*

*(A) Command economies have higher prices for oil. (B) Capitalist economies have higher prices for oil. (C) Command economies have a higher degree of government ownership of resources. (D) Capitalist economies have a higher degree of government ownership of resources. (E) Command economies rely on prices to allocate resources.*

The answer is **(C)**. The difference between the two systems is who owns and directs the scarce resources: in a command economy that is largely the government. The price of any single commodity, such as oil, is not what defines the system, which disposes of (A) and (B), and (D) reverses the ownership claim. (E) fails because relying on prices to allocate resources is the capitalist arrangement, not the command one — in a command economy the allocation is directed rather than priced.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Economics** | How society manages scarce resources |
| **Scarcity** | The limited nature of society's resources |
| **Microeconomics** | The study of how households and firms make decisions |
| **Macroeconomics** | The study of economy-wide phenomena — how a nation makes decisions |
| **Positive statement** | A descriptive statement; a statement of fact |
| **Normative statement** | A prescriptive statement; a statement of opinion |
| **Natural experiment** | An episode offered by history that economists analyse in place of a staged experiment |
| **Opportunity cost** | The second best alternative given up |
| **Marginal benefit and marginal cost** | The benefit and the cost of one more unit, which rational people compare when deciding |
| **Incentive** | Something that induces a person to act, either an award or a punishment |
| **Command economy** | An economy with a high degree of government ownership of resources, which does not rely on prices to allocate them |

# 2.1 Demand and Supply

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## Quantity demanded and the law of demand

**Quantity demanded (Qd)** is the amount of a good that buyers are willing and able to purchase. Both halves of that phrase matter: wanting the good is not enough, the buyer must also be able to pay for it.

The **law of demand** states that the quantity demanded of a good falls when the price of the good rises, other things equal. The final clause is what makes the law usable — it isolates the effect of price by holding everything else about the market still.

A **demand schedule** is a table that shows the relationship between the price of a good and the quantity demanded. The demand curve is that same relationship drawn out.

## What shifts demand

Everything the law of demand holds still is a possible shifter. When one of these changes, the whole demand curve moves, rather than the buyer sliding along it in response to a price change.

| Shifter | Effect |
|---|---|
| Number of buyers | An increase in the number of buyers increases demand |
| Income — **normal goods** | An increase in income increases demand, and a fall in income decreases it |
| Income — **inferior goods** | An increase in income decreases demand, and a fall in income increases it |
| **Substitutes** | An increase in the price of one causes an increase in demand for the other |
| **Complements** | An increase in the price of one causes a fall in demand for the other |
| Taste | Whether buyers favour a good or service over another or not |
| Expectations | If people expect incomes to rise, demand for goods increases now |

The distinction between normal and inferior goods is entirely about the direction of the income effect, and the distinction between substitutes and complements is entirely about the direction of the cross-price effect. Neither is a property of the good in isolation; both are statements about how demand for it responds.

## Quantity supplied and the law of supply

**Quantity supplied (Qs)** is the amount that sellers are willing and able to sell. The **law of supply** states that the quantity supplied of a good rises when the price of the good rises, other things equal — the mirror image of the law of demand, and for the mirror-image reason: a higher price makes selling more attractive to the seller, where it makes buying less attractive to the buyer.

A **supply schedule** is a table that shows the relationship between the price of a good and the quantity supplied.

## What shifts supply

| Shifter | Effect |
|---|---|
| Input price | A higher input price decreases supply |
| Technology | Better technology increases supply |
| Number of sellers | An increase in the number of sellers increases supply |
| Expectations | Sellers adjust supply when their expectations of future prices change |

## Worked example: a rival cuts its price

*Let BMW and Mercedes be the only two competitors in the automobile industry. All else equal, if Mercedes reduces the price of its cars, we should expect that*

*(A) BMW's supply curve will move to the left and the price of BMW cars will increase (B) BMW's supply curve will move to the right and the price of BMW cars will decrease (C) BMW's demand curve will move to the left and the price of BMW cars will decrease (D) BMW's demand curve will move to the right and the price of BMW cars will increase*

The answer is **(C)**. The two makes are substitutes, and the rule for substitutes is that an increase in the price of one causes an increase in demand for the other. Running it in the opposite direction, a *decrease* in the price of Mercedes causes a *decrease* in demand for BMW: buyers switch to the cheaper substitute. BMW's demand curve therefore moves left, and with less demand at every price the market price of BMW cars falls.

Options (A) and (B) fail before their price predictions are even considered, because they move the wrong curve. A rival's price is not one of the supply shifters — those are input prices, technology, the number of sellers and sellers' expectations — so nothing here touches BMW's supply.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Quantity demanded (Qd)** | The amount of a good that buyers are willing and able to purchase |
| **Law of demand** | The quantity demanded of a good falls when the price of the good rises, other things equal |
| **Demand schedule** | A table showing the relationship between the price of a good and the quantity demanded |
| **Normal good** | A good for which an increase in income increases demand |
| **Inferior good** | A good for which an increase in income decreases demand |
| **Substitutes** | Goods for which an increase in the price of one causes an increase in demand for the other |
| **Complements** | Goods for which an increase in the price of one causes a fall in demand for the other |
| **Quantity supplied (Qs)** | The amount that sellers are willing and able to sell |
| **Law of supply** | The quantity supplied of a good rises when the price of the good rises, other things equal |
| **Supply schedule** | A table showing the relationship between the price of a good and the quantity supplied |

# 3.1 Elasticity

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## What elasticity measures

**Elasticity** is the numerical measure of the responsiveness of quantity demanded or quantity supplied. The laws of demand and supply give the *direction* in which quantity moves when price changes; elasticity gives the *size* of that movement, which is what a firm or a government actually needs to know.

**Price elasticity of demand (PED)** measures how much quantity demanded responds to a change in price. It is calculated by the **midpoint method**.

**Price elasticity of supply (PES)** measures how much quantity supplied responds to a change in price.

## What determines price elasticity of demand

Four things determine how elastic demand for a good is:

- the **existence of substitutes**
- whether the good is a **necessity or a luxury**
- whether the good is **defined broadly or narrowly**
- whether the **long run or the short run** is being considered

The first of these connects straight back to the demand chapter. Substitutes were defined there as goods for which a rise in the price of one increases demand for the other; where such goods exist, a price rise can be answered by switching away, and quantity demanded therefore moves further than it would for a good with nowhere to switch to.

## Elasticity and the shape of the curve

The higher the elasticity, the flatter the curve is. A flat curve is one along which a small change in price is matched by a large change in quantity, which is exactly what a high elasticity says.

## Worked example: comparing two demand curves at a point

*Two straight-line demand curves intersect. How does the price elasticity of demand compare between these two curves at the point of intersection?*

*(A) The price elasticity is higher on the flatter curve than on the steeper curve. (B) The price elasticity is the same for both curves at the point of intersection. (C) The price elasticity is higher on the steeper curve than on the flatter curve. (D) The price elasticity is zero at the point of intersection for both curves. (E) The price elasticity is infinite at the point of intersection for both curves.*

The answer is **(A)**. At the point where the two curves cross, both describe the same price and the same quantity, so the only thing left to distinguish them is how far quantity moves when price moves — and that is the elasticity. The flatter curve delivers the larger change in quantity for a given change in price, so it is the more elastic there, which is the flatness rule above read in reverse.

The trap in this question is assuming that a shared point means shared elasticity, which is (B). Elasticity is a property of the *slope* through the point, not of the point itself.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Elasticity** | The numerical measure of the responsiveness of quantity demanded or quantity supplied |
| **Price elasticity of demand (PED)** | A measure of how much quantity demanded responds to a change in price |
| **Midpoint method** | The method used to calculate price elasticity of demand |
| **Price elasticity of supply (PES)** | A measure of how much quantity supplied responds to a change in price |

# 4.1 Price Controls and Taxes

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## Why governments control prices

A **price control** is a legally imposed limit on the price at which a good may trade. Its purpose is to deal with the inequalities generated within the market — the market clears at whatever price supply and demand produce, and that price may leave some buyers unable to afford a necessity or some sellers earning less than society is willing to tolerate.

There are two forms, distinguished only by which side of the market price they bind.

| Control | What it is | Standard example |
|---|---|---|
| **Price ceiling** | A legal maximum on the price | Rent-control laws |
| **Price floor** | A legal minimum on the price | Minimum wage laws |

A ceiling protects buyers: it stops the price rising above the stated maximum. A floor protects sellers, including sellers of labour: it stops the price falling below the stated minimum. In the labour market the seller is the worker, which is why the minimum wage is the standard example of a floor.

## Taxes

A **tax** serves two distinct purposes, and it is worth separating them because they pull a policy in different directions:

- to raise revenue for public purposes
- to influence market outcomes

The first treats the tax as a source of funds and is happiest when people go on buying the taxed good. The second treats the tax as a lever and succeeds precisely when people buy less of it. A tax designed to change behaviour and a tax designed to fill the treasury are not the same instrument, even when they are written the same way.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Price control** | A legal limit on price, imposed to deal with the inequalities generated within the market |
| **Price ceiling** | A legal maximum on the price, such as rent-control laws |
| **Price floor** | A legal minimum on the price, such as minimum wage laws |
| **Tax** | A charge used to raise revenue for public purposes and to influence market outcomes |

# 4.2 Externalities, Public Goods and Corrective Policy

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## When private incentives and social interest come apart

Most of this course assumes the parties to a trade bear its full cost and receive its full benefit. An **externality** is what happens when they do not: a cost or benefit of a transaction that falls on somebody who is neither the buyer nor the seller.

A **negative externality** is one where the third party bears a cost. The clearest example is pollution from a factory harming the health of people living nearby: the factory pays for its inputs and its customers pay for its output, but the neighbours pay in illness and are party to neither side of the deal. Oil leaking from drilling platforms in the Gulf of Mexico is the same structure — a cost imposed on people outside the transaction that produced it.

Several things that look similar are not externalities at all, and the practice set uses them as traps:

- **Bad weather reducing farmers' incomes.** Nobody's transaction caused it; it is a misfortune, not a spillover from a trade.
- **A rise in the price of oil**, whether it comes from environmental regulation or from action by a producers' organisation. A price change is how a market transmits information to its own participants; it is not a cost borne by an outsider.
- **A decline in oil stock prices from bad management.** The loss falls on the owners of the firm, who are parties to it.

## The socially optimal quantity

Because an externality drives a wedge between private and social accounts, four separate curves are needed to describe such a market:

| Curve | What it measures |
|---|---|
| **Marginal private cost (MPC)** | The cost to the producer of one more unit |
| **Marginal social cost (MSC)** | The cost to society as a whole of one more unit |
| **Marginal private benefit (MPB)** | The benefit to the consumer of one more unit |
| **Marginal social benefit (MSB)** | The benefit to society as a whole of one more unit |

The market equilibrium quantity is set where private cost meets private benefit, because that is what the two parties respond to. The **socially optimal quantity** is set where **marginal social cost equals marginal social benefit**. Where an externality exists these two quantities differ, and the gap between them is the inefficiency. The same condition defines the socially optimal quantity of a **public good**: it is provided in the right amount when marginal social cost equals marginal social benefit, not when private cost equals private benefit and not at any comparison of *totals* — the decision is always about one more unit.

## Correcting a negative externality

The policy used to control a negative externality is a **tax**. A tax on the activity raises the private cost of each unit towards its social cost, so the quantity chosen privately moves towards the socially optimal quantity. This is the second purpose of taxation — influencing market outcomes — doing the work it was described as doing.

The choice of instrument decides whether the correction actually happens:

- A **per-unit tax** changes the cost of every additional unit, so it changes the marginal calculation that sets quantity.
- A **lump-sum tax** is a fixed charge that does not vary with output or consumption. It takes money but leaves the cost of one more unit untouched, so it does not move quantity. This is why a lump-sum tax on a monopolist does not reduce the inefficiency of monopoly: it transfers money without changing the firm's marginal decision.
- A **subsidy** works in the opposite direction, increasing the quantity — so subsidising the consumption of a good produced by a polluting plant makes the inefficiency worse, not better.

Direction matters as much as instrument. Taxing a chocolate factory whose aroma the residents of the city enjoy attacks a *benefit* that spills over rather than a cost, and reduces an activity society would prefer more of.

## Worked example: which government action reduces inefficiency

*In which of the following cases is the government's action appropriate for reducing inefficiency?*

*(A) Taxation of the output of a chocolate factory that emits an aroma that residents of the city enjoy (B) Regulation that reduces the output of a monopoly (C) A lump-sum tax on a monopolist (D) A subsidy for the consumption of a good produced by a plant that emits a pollutant as a by-product (E) A toll on a congested bridge*

The answer is **(E)**. Each extra driver on a congested bridge slows every other driver down — a cost imposed on people outside that driver's own decision. A toll is a per-unit charge for crossing, so it raises the private cost of the crossing towards its social cost and reduces the number of crossings towards the optimum.

The others fail on the tests above: (A) taxes a spillover benefit; (D) subsidises a polluting activity, moving quantity the wrong way; (C) leaves the monopolist's marginal decision unchanged; and (B) reduces the output of a monopoly that is already producing too little.

## Worked example: sugar, health and the right instrument

The free-response question sets a perfectly competitive sugar market and then supposes that *sugar consumption has a negative impact on public health over time, and the negative impact of sugar on health is underestimated by consumers.*

Because consumers underestimate the harm, the benefit they perceive from a unit of sugar exceeds the benefit society actually gets from it: marginal private benefit lies above marginal social benefit. Buyers trade until private benefit meets private cost, so the **market equilibrium quantity $Q_M$ is larger than the socially optimal quantity $Q_S$**, which is where marginal social cost meets marginal social benefit. Sugar is over-consumed relative to the optimum.

The question then asks which of a lump-sum tax, a per-unit tax, a lump-sum subsidy or a per-unit subsidy would best affect consumers' incentives in the short run. The answer is the **per-unit tax**. Only a per-unit charge alters the cost of the next unit of sugar, which is the quantity decision the policy needs to reach; a lump-sum tax leaves that decision untouched, and either subsidy pushes consumption further above $Q_S$ rather than towards it.

The graphs this question asks for did not survive into the text of the practice set, so draw them yourself from the relationships stated here: with the harm underestimated by consumers, it is the benefit curves that separate.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Externality** | A cost or benefit of a transaction falling on somebody who is neither the buyer nor the seller |
| **Negative externality** | An externality that imposes a cost on a third party, such as pollution from a factory on the health of people living nearby |
| **Marginal private cost (MPC)** | The cost to the producer of one more unit |
| **Marginal social cost (MSC)** | The cost to society as a whole of one more unit |
| **Marginal private benefit (MPB)** | The benefit to the consumer of one more unit |
| **Marginal social benefit (MSB)** | The benefit to society as a whole of one more unit |
| **Socially optimal quantity** | The quantity at which marginal social cost equals marginal social benefit |
| **Per-unit tax** | A tax charged on every unit, which changes the cost of one more unit and so changes quantity |
| **Lump-sum tax** | A fixed charge that does not vary with output, and so does not change the quantity decision |

# 5.1 Welfare Economics: Consumer, Producer and Total Surplus

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## What welfare economics asks

**Welfare economics** is the study of how the allocation of resources affects economic well-being. It takes the outcome a market produces and asks whether that outcome is good for the people in it, which is a different question from asking what the outcome will be.

**Economic well-being** is a person's or family's standard of living, based primarily on how well they are doing financially. Across a whole country it can be calculated by GDP per capita.

An allocation of resources is settled by three separate decisions:

- how much of each good is produced
- which producers produce it
- which consumers consume it

A market answers all three at once through its price, and welfare economics is the measurement of how well it answered them.

## Consumer surplus

**Consumer surplus (CS)** is the amount a buyer is willing to pay minus the amount the buyer pays. It is the gain the buyer walks away with: a buyer prepared to pay 30 for a good that costs 20 is better off by 10 for having been able to trade at the market price rather than at the most they would have borne.

Buyers who are willing to pay less than the price simply do not buy, so no buyer ever has negative consumer surplus. Everyone who trades gains something, or they would not have traded.

## Producer surplus

**Producer surplus (PS)** is the amount a seller is paid for a good minus the seller's cost:

$$PS = P - \text{cost}$$

The logic is the mirror image of consumer surplus. A seller whose cost exceeds the price does not sell, so a seller who does sell is better off by the difference between the price received and what the good cost them to provide.

## Total surplus

**Total surplus (TS)** is the two added together:

$$TS = CS + PS$$

Total surplus is the total gains from trade in a market — everything both sides of the market gained by trading rather than not trading. It is the number welfare economics uses to judge an allocation, because it counts the gain to buyers and the gain to sellers on the same scale, and so allows a policy that helps one side at the expense of the other to be assessed as a whole.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Welfare economics** | The study of how the allocation of resources affects economic well-being |
| **Economic well-being** | A person's or family's standard of living, based primarily on how well they are doing financially; across a country it can be calculated by GDP per capita |
| **Consumer surplus (CS)** | The amount a buyer is willing to pay minus the amount the buyer pays |
| **Producer surplus (PS)** | The amount a seller is paid for a good minus the seller's cost, $PS = P - \text{cost}$ |
| **Total surplus (TS)** | $TS = CS + PS$; the total gains from trade in a market |

# 6.1 Explicit and Implicit Costs, and the Two Kinds of Profit

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## Two kinds of cost

**Explicit cost** is the cost that involves the actual outlay of money — wages paid, rent paid, materials bought. If money changed hands, the cost is explicit.

**Implicit cost** is the measure of the value of the forgone benefits: the opportunity costs and trade-offs a decision carries. No money leaves the firm, but something of value was given up all the same.

The two together are what a decision really costs:

$$\text{explicit cost} + \text{implicit cost} = \text{total opportunity cost}$$

This is the first principle of economics applied to a firm. The cost of something is what you give up, and what you give up is not confined to what you paid for.

## Two kinds of profit

Because there are two kinds of cost, there are two kinds of profit, and they differ by exactly the costs one of them ignores.

| | Definition | Formula |
|---|---|---|
| **Accounting profit** | The business's revenue minus the explicit costs and depreciation | $R - \text{explicit cost} - \text{depreciation}$ |
| **Economic profit** | The business's revenue minus the opportunity cost | $R - \text{explicit cost} - OC$ |

The guide prints the accounting-profit formula as $R - \text{explicit cost}$, dropping depreciation; that is an error — depreciation belongs in the formula, as the guide's own definition of the term says. Economic profit is often less than accounting profit, and the reason is visible in the two formulas: economic profit subtracts the opportunity cost of the resources the owner supplies, which accounting profit never sees. Whenever an owner has a valuable alternative use for their time or their capital, the accounts will look healthier than the economics.

**Capital** is the value of a firm's assets — equipment, buildings, tools, inventory and financial assets.

**Normal profit** is a zero economic profit: just enough to keep the resources the firm employs in its current activity. Zero economic profit sounds like failure and is not. It means the firm is earning precisely what its resources could earn in their next best use, so there is no reason to move them, and no reason to bring more in.

## Worked example: a forgone salary

*An entrepreneur leaves a £50,000/year job to start a business. The lost salary is an example of:*

*(A) An explicit cost, because it was a direct monetary payment. (B) An accounting cost, because it appears on financial statements. (C) An implicit cost, because it represents an opportunity cost. (D) An opportunity cost, because it represents the sum of all of the alternative decisions the entrepreneur could have made. (E) An investment cost, because it causes the entrepreneur to take the risk of not getting a larger or equal amount of profit.*

The answer is **(C)**. The business never writes a cheque for the salary; the entrepreneur simply stops receiving one. Nothing is paid out, so the cost is not explicit, which rules out (A) and (B) together — a cost with no outlay does not appear on the financial statements either.

(D) is the more interesting distractor, because the salary *is* an opportunity cost. The reason it fails is its explanation: opportunity cost is the second best alternative given up, not the sum of every alternative the entrepreneur could have chosen.

## Worked example: computing economic profit

*Bruce is a talented writer and graphic artist who enjoys both types of work equally. Instead of earning \$45,000 as a writer, Bruce now earns \$25,000 in accounting profits as a graphic artist using the same computer he would have used as a writer. What is Bruce's economic profit from choosing to work as a graphic artist?*

*(A) -\$45,000 (B) -\$20,000 (C) \$20,000 (D) \$45,000 (E) \$70,000*

The answer is **(B)**. Start from the accounting profit he actually earns, \$25,000, and subtract the opportunity cost of earning it — the \$45,000 he gave up by not writing:

$$\$25{,}000 - \$45{,}000 = -\$20{,}000$$

Two details in the question exist to be ruled out of the calculation. He would have used the same computer either way, so the computer is not part of what he gave up by choosing one occupation over the other. And he enjoys both kinds of work equally, so there is no non-monetary benefit to add on either side. That leaves the salary as the whole of the implicit cost.

A negative economic profit does not mean Bruce is losing money — his accounting profit is a positive \$25,000. It means he is \$20,000 worse off than he would have been in his best alternative, which is the judgement economic profit is built to deliver.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Explicit cost** | The cost that involves the actual outlay of money |
| **Implicit cost** | The measure of the value of the forgone benefits — opportunity costs, trade-offs and the like |
| **Total opportunity cost** | Explicit cost plus implicit cost |
| **Accounting profit** | The business's revenue minus the explicit costs and depreciation |
| **Economic profit** | The business's revenue minus the opportunity cost; often less than the accounting profit |
| **Capital** | The value of a firm's assets, such as equipment, buildings, tools, inventory and financial assets |
| **Normal profit** | A zero economic profit — just enough to keep the resources a firm employs in its current activity |

# 7.1 The Production Possibility Curve, Marginal Utility and the Optimal Output Rule

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## The production possibility curve

The **production possibility curve (PPC)** shows what an economy can produce with the resources it has — capital, land and labour. Because those resources are scarce, the curve has an edge, and the position of a production point relative to that edge is the whole of what the diagram says:

| Position | Meaning |
|---|---|
| Inside the curve | Inefficient — resources are available but are not all being used |
| On the curve | Efficient |
| Outside the curve | Impossible |

Efficiency here is not a judgement about which point on the curve is the right one. Every point on the curve is efficient; choosing between them is the trade-off, and moving from one to another means giving something up. The curve is the first principle of economics drawn as a picture.

The guide's diagram of the curve did not survive into the extracted text, so the axes and the shape are not reproduced here. What the guide states about it is the three-way classification above.

## Marginal utility

**Marginal utility** is the additional utility from consuming one more unit of that good or service. The guide prints the definition as the utility from spending one more dollar on the good; that is an error — marginal utility is measured per additional unit, and it is the division by price on the next line that turns it into utility per dollar. Dividing it by price gives the quantity a consumer can actually act on:

$$\frac{\text{marginal utility of one unit}}{\text{price of one unit of the good}} = \frac{MU_{good}}{P_{good}} = \text{marginal utility per unit}$$

The guide prints this ratio a second time with "total utility" on the right-hand side; go by the definition given above, which the consumer-equilibrium question below also bears out.

The point of dividing by price is comparability. Marginal utilities on their own cannot be compared across goods that cost different amounts, because a large utility bought at a large price may be a worse use of money than a small utility bought cheaply. The ratio puts every good on the same footing: utility per unit of money spent.

## The optimal output rule

| Rule | Condition |
|---|---|
| **Optimal output rule** | Profit is maximised by producing the quantity of output at which the marginal cost of the last unit produced is equal to its marginal revenue |
| **Firm's optimal output rule** | The firm's profit is maximised by producing the quantity of output at which the marginal cost of the last unit produced is equal to the market price |

Both are the same idea — keep producing while the last unit brings in more than it costs, and stop when the two are equal. The second is the first as it applies to a firm that takes the market price as given, since for such a firm the revenue from one more unit simply *is* the market price.

## Worked example: consumer equilibrium

*Suppose that Jamal purchases two goods X and Y. The marginal utility of X is $MU_x$, the total utility of X is $TU_x$, the marginal utility of Y is $MU_y$, and the total utility of Y is $TU_y$. If the prices of X and Y are $P_x$ and $P_y$ respectively, which of the following expressions defines consumer equilibrium?*

*(A) $TU_x = TU_y$ (B) $MU_x = MU_y$ (C) $TU_x/P_x = TU_y/P_y$ (D) $MU_x/P_x = MU_y/P_y$ (E) $(MU_x)(P_x) + (MU_y)(P_y) = 1$*

The answer is **(D)**. Consumer equilibrium is the condition in which the marginal utility per unit of money is the same in both uses. If it were not — if $MU_x/P_x$ exceeded $MU_y/P_y$ — then moving the next dollar from Y to X would buy more utility than it gave up, so Jamal would not yet be doing the best he can. Only when the two ratios are equal is there nothing left to gain by shifting spending, which is what the third principle of economics, thinking at the margin, requires.

The distractors each drop one of the two ingredients. (A) and (C) work with total utility rather than marginal utility, so they compare whole stocks of satisfaction instead of the next unit. (B) uses marginal utility but ignores the prices, and so treats a dollar's worth of an expensive good as equivalent to a dollar's worth of a cheap one.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Production possibility curve (PPC)** | The curve showing what can be produced from an economy's resources: points inside are inefficient, points on the curve are efficient, points outside are impossible |
| **Marginal utility** | The additional utility from consuming one more unit of that good or service |
| **Marginal utility per unit** | Marginal utility of one unit divided by the price of one unit, $MU_{good}/P_{good}$ |
| **Consumer equilibrium** | The condition $MU_x/P_x = MU_y/P_y$, in which the marginal utility per unit of money is equal across goods |
| **Optimal output rule** | Profit is maximised by producing the quantity of output at which the marginal cost of the last unit produced equals its marginal revenue |
| **Firm's optimal output rule** | The firm's profit is maximised by producing the quantity of output at which the marginal cost of the last unit produced equals the market price |

# 8.1 Production and Costs in the Short and Long Run

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## Fixed and variable inputs

A **fixed input** is an input whose quantity is fixed for a period of time and cannot be varied. A **variable input** is an input whose quantity the firm can vary at any time.

The two run directly into the definition of the two time horizons, which in economics are defined by what can be changed rather than by any number of months:

| Horizon | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Short run** | The time period in which at least one input is fixed |
| **Long run** | The time period in which all inputs can be varied |

A firm in the short run is a firm stuck with something — a factory, a lease, a machine — and most of the cost structure below is a consequence of being stuck with it.

## The total product curve and marginal product

The **total product curve** shows how the quantity of output depends on the quantity of a variable input, for a given quantity of the fixed input.

**Marginal product** is the additional quantity of output that is produced by using one more unit of input:

$$MP = \frac{\Delta Q_{output}}{\Delta Q_{input}} \qquad MP_L = \frac{\Delta Q}{\Delta L}$$

Marginal product diminishes as the input increases. This is the single most consequential fact in the topic: as more of the variable input is piled onto the same fixed input, each additional unit of input has less of the fixed input to work with, and so adds less output than the one before it.

## Costs

**Fixed cost** is the cost that does not depend on the quantity of output produced. **Variable cost** is the cost that does depend on the quantity of output produced. Together they are the **total cost** of that quantity of output:

$$TC = FC + VC$$

The total cost curve becomes steeper as more output is produced, and this is diminishing returns showing up in money. Since each extra unit of output requires more additional input than the last one did, it also costs more than the last one did.

## The cost measures

| Measure | Formula | What it is |
|---|---|---|
| **Total cost (TC)** | $TC = FC + VC$ | The sum of fixed and variable cost at that quantity of output |
| **Marginal cost (MC)** | $MC = \dfrac{\Delta TC}{\Delta Q}$ | The addition to total cost from one more unit of output |
| **Average total cost (ATC)** | $ATC = \dfrac{TC}{Q}$ | Total cost divided by quantity of output |
| **Average fixed cost (AFC)** | $AFC = \dfrac{FC}{Q}$ | Fixed cost per unit of output |

Average total cost is U-shaped: it falls at low levels of output, then rises. The fall comes from the fixed cost being spread over more units — $AFC = FC/Q$ shrinks as $Q$ grows — and the rise comes from diminishing returns eventually pushing marginal cost above the average and dragging it up.

## Worked example: marginal cost from marginal product

*If labour is the only variable input and it costs \$15 per hour, and if the marginal product of labour is 3 units per hour, the short-run marginal cost of 1 unit of output is approximately*

*(A) \$0.20 (B) \$3.00 (C) \$5.00 (D) \$15.00 (E) \$45.00*

The answer is **(C)**. An hour of labour costs \$15 and yields 3 units of output, so the cost attributable to one unit is

$$MC = \frac{\Delta TC}{\Delta Q} = \frac{\$15}{3\ \text{units}} = \$5\ \text{per unit}$$

The two wrong answers worth naming are (D), which reports the cost of the *input* rather than of a unit of output, and (E), which multiplies the wage by the marginal product instead of dividing. The check on the arithmetic is the direction of the effect: a more productive worker should make output cheaper, so a rise in marginal product must push marginal cost down, which only division does.

## Worked example: average total cost from average product

*Assume that total fixed costs are \$46, that the average product of labour is 5 units when 10 units of output are produced, and that the wage rate is \$12. If labour is the only variable input, what is the average total cost of producing 10 units of output?*

*(A) \$2 (B) \$5 (C) \$7 (D) \$9 (E) \$12*

The answer is **(C)**. Work backwards from the average product to the labour actually employed. **Average product** is output per unit of labour, so if 10 units of output are produced at an average product of 5, the firm is using

$$L = \frac{10}{5} = 2 \text{ units of labour}$$

Labour is the only variable input, so variable cost is the wage bill:

$$VC = 2 \times \$12 = \$24$$

$$TC = FC + VC = \$46 + \$24 = \$70$$

$$ATC = \frac{TC}{Q} = \frac{\$70}{10} = \$7$$

The order of operations is what this question is testing: average product converts output into an input requirement, the wage converts the input requirement into variable cost, and only then can fixed cost be added and the total divided by output.

## Worked example: from average variable cost to total variable cost

One further question gives the average variable cost as \$60 for an output of 11 units and asks what follows. The step it depends on is that an average multiplied by the quantity returns the total:

$$VC = AVC \times Q = \$60 \times 11 = \$660$$

So total variable cost at 11 units is \$660, not \$630, and \$660 is the *variable* cost rather than the total cost — total cost would be \$660 plus whatever the fixed cost is. The answer key gives the marginal cost of the eleventh unit, \$190, as the correct option; that figure has to be read off the cost table printed with the question, since marginal cost is the difference $TC_{11} - TC_{10}$ and the table is what supplies $TC_{10}$. The table did not survive into the extracted text, so only the average-to-total step above can be reconstructed here.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Fixed input** | An input whose quantity is fixed for a period of time and cannot be varied |
| **Variable input** | An input whose quantity the firm can vary at any time |
| **Short run** | The time period in which at least one input is fixed |
| **Long run** | The time period in which all inputs can be varied |
| **Total product curve** | A curve showing how the quantity of output depends on the quantity of a variable input, for a given fixed input |
| **Marginal product** | The additional quantity of output produced by using one more unit of input, $MP_L = \Delta Q/\Delta L$ |
| **Average product** | Output per unit of the input employed |
| **Fixed cost** | The cost that does not depend on the quantity of output produced |
| **Variable cost** | The cost that depends on the quantity of output produced |
| **Total cost (TC)** | The sum of fixed cost and variable cost of producing that quantity of output |
| **Marginal cost (MC)** | The change in total cost divided by the change in output |
| **Average total cost (ATC)** | Total cost divided by quantity of output; U-shaped, falling at low output then rising |
| **Average fixed cost (AFC)** | Fixed cost per unit of output |

# 9.1 Revenue, Profit and the Break-Even Price

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## Marginal revenue

The **marginal revenue** curve shows how marginal revenue varies as output varies — that is, how much the firm gains in revenue from selling one more unit, at each level of output. It is the revenue side of the comparison the optimal output rule makes, marginal cost being the other side.

## Whether the firm is making money

Profitability is settled by comparing total revenue with total cost:

| Comparison | Outcome |
|---|---|
| $TR > TC$ | The firm is profitable |
| $TR = TC$ | The firm breaks even |
| $TR < TC$ | The firm incurs a loss |

This tells the firm whether to be in business at all. It does not tell it how much to produce — that is what the marginal comparison does. Keeping the two questions apart is the point of having both a total and a marginal test.

## The break-even price

The **break-even price** is the market price at which the firm earns zero profits. Because average total cost is cost per unit and price is revenue per unit, the break-even price is the minimum of the average total cost curve, and the three cases follow immediately:

| Market price | Result |
|---|---|
| Market price > minimum ATC | Profitable |
| Market price = minimum ATC | Breaks even |
| Market price < minimum ATC | Unprofitable |

The minimum of ATC is used rather than any other point on the curve because the firm gets to choose its output. If price is above the lowest average total cost the firm can achieve, there is some quantity at which revenue per unit beats cost per unit; if price is below it, there is none.

## Worked example: price above marginal cost

*If a perfectly competitive firm wishes to maximise profits and is producing where price exceeds both marginal cost and average variable cost, then the firm is*

*(A) producing too little output (B) producing where its marginal revenue is less than its marginal cost (C) using too much of the variable input (D) charging too high a price for its output (E) not earning any economic profits*

The answer is **(A)**. For a firm in a perfectly competitive market the firm's optimal output rule sets marginal cost equal to the market price. Here price is *above* marginal cost, so the last unit produced added more to revenue than it added to cost, and so would the next one. The firm has not yet produced enough, and expanding output raises profit until marginal cost has risen to meet the price.

(B) describes the opposite error — marginal revenue below marginal cost is the signal to produce less, not more — and (C) is that same error stated in terms of the input. (D) is impossible for a perfectly competitive firm, which is a price taker and does not set its price at all. (E) confuses the marginal condition with the profitability test: whether economic profit exists depends on price against minimum average total cost, which this question never gives.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Marginal revenue** | The revenue from one more unit of output; its curve shows how marginal revenue varies as output varies |
| **Break-even price** | The market price at which a firm earns zero profits, equal to its minimum average total cost |

# 9.2 Market Structures

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## The four structures

Market structures are classified by three things: how many firms there are, whether their products are identical or differentiated, and whether new firms can enter.

| Structure | Number of firms | Product | Entry |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Perfect competition** | Many, all price-takers | Identical | Free entry and exit, no barriers |
| **Monopoly** | One | No close substitutes | Barriers to entry |
| **Oligopoly** | A small number of large firms | — | Barriers to entry |
| **Monopolistic competition** | Large numbers | Differentiated | Free entry and exit in the long run |

Every result in this topic follows from those three columns, so it is worth reading the table as a set of causes rather than a set of labels.

## Perfect competition

Firms in perfect competition are **price-takers**: they accept the market price rather than setting it. There is free entry and exit, and there are no barriers.

The reason firms are price-takers is that each one is too small to influence the market price on its own. That, and not any agreement or regulation, is what removes their pricing power — which is why a perfectly competitive firm producing identical output alongside many others has nothing to gain by charging more, since buyers can get the same good elsewhere.

*Which of the following is a characteristic of firms in a perfectly competitive industry? (A) Engaging in collusive behaviour (B) Facing significant barriers to entry (C) Setting the market price (D) Producing identical products (E) Earning long-run economic profit*

The answer is **(D)**. Each of the other four options contradicts one of the three defining columns: collusion and price-setting both require the market power that price-takers lack, barriers to entry contradict free entry, and long-run economic profit is competed away precisely because entry is free.

## Monopoly

A **monopoly** is an industry controlled by a monopolist, selling a good with no close substitutes. What keeps it a monopoly is that other firms cannot get in, and the guide gives four kinds of **barrier to entry**:

| Barrier | |
|---|---|
| Control of a scarce resource or input | The entrant cannot obtain what it would need to produce |
| Economies of scale | The incumbent's costs per unit fall with size, so a small entrant cannot match its prices |
| Technological superiority | The incumbent can do something the entrant cannot |
| Government created barriers | Entry is restricted by law |

## Oligopoly: interdependence and game theory

An **oligopoly** is a market with a small number of large firms. Its three characteristics are a few large firms, barriers to entry, and **interdependence** — each firm's best action depends on what the others do, because with only a handful of firms, one firm's price change is large enough to matter to the rest.

Interdependence is why oligopoly is often analysed with **game theory**, and it is the answer to the question of where game theory is useful:

*Game theory is most useful in describing outcomes in markets in which (A) firms are price takers (B) there is only one producer (C) there are many small producers (D) products are identical for all firms (E) there are interdependent firms*

The answer is **(E)**. Game theory analyses decisions that depend on other people's decisions. A price-taker among many small producers has nobody in particular to respond to, and a single producer has no rival at all; only interdependence gives the analysis something to work on.

The practice set names two ways oligopolists may compete with one another:

| Model | How firms compete |
|---|---|
| **Bertrand oligopoly** | Firms compete with each other by setting the price |
| **Cournot oligopoly** | Firms compete with each other by choosing the production quantity |

### The kinked demand curve

*The kinked demand curve model of oligopoly suggests that firms: (A) Ignore competitors' pricing decisions. (B) Match price cuts but not price increases, leading to price rigidity. (C) Always act as price takers. (D) Produce at minimum average total cost in the long run. (E) Are likely to become monopoly*

The answer is **(B)**. The model assumes each firm expects its rivals to follow a price cut but not a price rise. A firm that raises its price is therefore left alone at the higher price and loses customers to the rivals who stayed put; a firm that cuts its price finds the cut matched and gains little. Both moves look unattractive, so prices tend not to move at all — **price rigidity**. Note that (A) states the opposite of interdependence, and (C) belongs to perfect competition.

### Why collusion does not last

*Which of the following best explains why it is difficult to maintain lasting collusive agreements? (A) There is an unavoidable conflict in that a collusive agreement can increase the profits of some, but not all, firms in the industry. (B) There is little potential for gain from collusion unless there is a large number of consumers in the market. (C) Each firm in the industry views itself as facing a vertical demand curve, even though the market demand curve is downward sloping. (D) The firms in the industry have a common incentive to increase output to a more competitive level. (E) Each firm realises that its profits would increase if it were the only firm to violate the collusive agreement by increasing its production slightly.*

The answer is **(E)**, and it is a statement about incentives rather than about honesty. **Collusion** raises profits by restricting output between the firms, but the restriction is exactly what makes cheating attractive: with the price held up by everybody else's restraint, one firm selling a little more captures the gain while the others carry the cost. Every firm faces that calculation, which is why the agreement is unstable from the inside. (D) inverts the point — firms have a common incentive to *restrict* output, and an individual incentive to expand.

### Nash equilibrium in a symmetric game

The practice set also sets a rock-paper-scissors game and asks which statement about it is true, offering: that losing is just as hard as winning; that the game has one pure-strategy **Nash equilibrium**; that it has three such equilibria each with a payoff of (0 : 0); or that it has no equilibrium in pure or mixed strategies.

The answer key gives the first. A pure-strategy Nash equilibrium is a pair of choices that neither player would want to move away from, given what the other has chosen — and rock-paper-scissors has none, because whichever pair is named, the loser of that pair would rather have chosen differently. That disposes of the second and third options. The remaining claim is the symmetry of the game: each of the three choices beats one of the others and loses to one, so no strategy makes winning easier than losing.

The payoff table printed with the question did not survive into the extracted text, so the reasoning above rests on the structure of the game as the question names it.

## Monopolistic competition

**Monopolistic competition** combines large numbers of firms with **differentiated products** and free entry and exit in the long run. The differentiation gives each firm a little pricing power over its own version of the product; the free entry takes the profits away again.

*In the long run, firms in monopolistic competition typically earn (A) Economic profits due to barriers to entry. (B) Zero economic profits due to free entry and competition. (C) Losses because of excessive advertising costs. (D) Monopoly-level supernormal profits. (E) infinite profit*

The answer is **(B)**. Free entry is the operative feature. If firms in the market are earning economic profits, new firms enter and take a share of the demand, and entry continues until there is no economic profit left to attract anyone — the normal profit of the costs lesson, and the break-even condition of the previous lesson. (A) and (D) both assume barriers that this structure does not have.

*In monopolistic competition, advertising is primarily used to: (A) Lower production costs through economies of scale. (B) Make demand curves perfectly inelastic. (C) Create brand loyalty and perceived product differentiation. (D) Comply with government regulations. (E) Decrease profit*

The answer is **(C)**. Differentiation is what a firm in this structure competes on, and advertising is how differentiation is manufactured and maintained: it persuades buyers that this version is not interchangeable with the others. Note that (C) says *perceived* differentiation — the advertising need not change the product to change the demand for it.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Perfect competition** | A market of price-taking firms with free entry and exit and no barriers, producing identical products |
| **Price-taker** | A firm that accepts the market price rather than setting it, because it is too small to influence that price |
| **Monopoly** | An industry controlled by a monopolist, whose good has no close substitutes and which is protected by barriers to entry |
| **Barriers to entry** | Control of a scarce resource or input, economies of scale, technological superiority, and government created barriers |
| **Oligopoly** | A market with a small number of large firms, barriers to entry and interdependence |
| **Interdependence** | The condition in which each firm's best action depends on what the other firms do |
| **Bertrand oligopoly** | A market in which oligopolists compete with each other by setting the price |
| **Cournot oligopoly** | A market in which oligopolists compete with each other by choosing the production quantity |
| **Kinked demand curve model** | The oligopoly model in which firms match price cuts but not price increases, leading to price rigidity |
| **Collusion** | An agreement between firms to restrict output, unstable because each firm gains by violating it alone |
| **Nash equilibrium** | A combination of choices from which neither player would want to move, given the other's choice |
| **Monopolistic competition** | A market with large numbers of firms, differentiated products, and free entry and exit in the long run |

# 10.1 Industry Supply and Long-Run Equilibrium

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## The industry supply curve

The **industry supply curve** shows the relationship between the price of goods and the total output of the industry as a whole. It is the market-level counterpart of the single firm's supply decision: each firm decides how much to produce at the going price, and the industry curve adds those decisions up.

**Short-run market equilibrium** is the price at which quantity supplied equals quantity demanded, with the number of firms in the industry taken as given.

## The long-run industry supply curve

The **long-run industry supply curve** is the industry supply curve given sufficient time for entry into and exit from the industry. **Long-run market equilibrium** is again the price at which quantity supplied equals the quantity demanded — but now with the number of firms free to change.

The difference between the two is entry and exit, and it is what makes the long run behave differently from the short run. In the short run a price rise makes existing firms profitable and they stay profitable, because nobody else can get in yet. In the long run those profits are a signal, new firms act on it, and the industry's output rises by more than the existing firms alone could have raised it.

## Worked example: the sugar market adjusting to a rise in demand

The free-response question sets sugar in a perfectly competitive market, with inputs bought from perfectly competitive factor markets, and Frank Sugar Co. as a representative firm in it. The graphs it asks for are drawn side by side — the market on one, the firm on the other — and the parts below give the relationships those graphs have to show.

**(a) The firm is earning zero economic profit.** The market equilibrium price and quantity $P_M$ and $Q_M$ sit where the market's supply and demand curves cross. The firm is a price-taker, so the profit-maximising price for Frank Sugar Co. is not a separate decision: it is $P_M$. The firm's profit-maximising quantity $Q_F$ is the one at which its marginal cost equals that price, following the firm's optimal output rule. Zero economic profit adds one more condition, since the break-even price is the minimum of average total cost: the firm must be at the bottom of its ATC curve, with $P_M$ equal to minimum ATC.

**(b)(i) Demand for sugar increases.** The market demand curve shifts right, so the market price rises to $P_2$. Frank Sugar Co. still takes the price as given, and still produces where marginal cost equals it — but marginal cost rises with output, so the quantity that satisfies $MC = P_2$ is larger than $Q_F$. The firm's quantity $Q_N$ therefore exceeds $Q_F$.

**(b)(ii) What happens to the firm's short-run profit?** It rises. The firm was earning zero economic profit at a price equal to its minimum average total cost, and the price is now above that minimum, which is the profitable case of the break-even test. The firm earns a positive economic profit in the short run.

**(b)(iii) How will the long-run price compare to $P_2$?** It will be **lower than $P_2$**. Positive economic profits are what free entry responds to: sugar is a perfectly competitive market, so new firms enter, industry supply increases, and the price falls. Entry only stops when there is no economic profit left to attract it, which means when price has come back down to minimum average total cost. Sugar is stated to be a **constant-cost industry** — one whose costs per unit do not change as the industry expands — so that minimum is the same as it was before, and the long-run price returns to the original $P_M$.

The graphs cannot be reproduced here, since no figure from the practice set survived into the extracted text. Draw them from the relationships above, which is what the question is testing in any case: the firm's price is the market's price, its quantity is set by $MC = P$, and zero profit puts that intersection at the bottom of ATC.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Industry supply curve** | The curve showing the relationship between the price of goods and the total output of the industry as a whole |
| **Short-run market equilibrium** | The point at which quantity supplied equals quantity demanded, with the number of firms fixed |
| **Long-run industry supply curve** | The industry supply curve given sufficient time for entry into and exit from the industry |
| **Long-run market equilibrium** | The point at which quantity supplied equals quantity demanded once entry and exit have run their course |
| **Constant-cost industry** | An industry whose costs per unit do not change as the industry expands |

# 10.2 Monopoly and Market Power

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## The monopolist's demand curve

A monopolist is the industry, so the demand curve it faces is the market demand curve, and it slopes downward. Selling one more unit therefore has two consequences at once, and the guide separates them:

| Effect | What it does to total revenue |
|---|---|
| **Quantity effect** | One more unit is sold, increasing total revenue by the price at which that unit is sold |
| **Price effect** | To sell the last unit, the monopolist must cut the market price on all units sold, which decreases total revenue |

A firm with no market power has only the quantity effect to consider, because it can sell as much as it likes at the going price. The price effect is what market power costs the firm that holds it, and it is the source of every difference between monopoly and competition that follows.

Because the price effect subtracts from the quantity effect, the revenue gained from one more unit is less than the price that unit sells for. The firm stops producing when $MC = MR$ — the optimal output rule — and since marginal revenue is below the price, the price at that quantity is above marginal cost.

## Market power and efficiency

*The condition for allocative efficiency is violated when (A) firms are price makers (price searchers) (B) short-run profits exist in a competitive industry (C) price equals average total cost (D) the market demand curve is inelastic in a competitive industry (E) the market demand curve is elastic in a competitive industry*

The answer is **(A)**. Allocative efficiency requires the price of the last unit to equal the marginal cost of producing it, so that what buyers pay for one more unit matches what society gives up to make it. A price maker faces a downward-sloping demand curve and so faces the price effect, which puts marginal revenue below price; producing where $MC = MR$ therefore leaves price above marginal cost, and the condition fails. The elasticity of demand in a *competitive* industry, options (D) and (E), does not bear on the condition at all, since firms there set marginal cost equal to the price whatever the elasticity.

The same reasoning answers the question of what can be said about the quantity a producer with market power chooses:

*If a producer has market power (that is, with her actions she can influence the market price), what can we say about the quantity produced? (A) It is equitable (B) It is efficient (C) It maximises consumer surplus (D) None of the other answers is correct*

The answer is **(D)**. The quantity is not efficient, for the reason just given. It does not maximise consumer surplus either — consumer surplus is willingness to pay minus the amount paid, and market power works by holding the price up and the quantity down, which cuts into both. And nothing about market power settles the question of equity one way or the other.

## Worked example: a per-unit tax on a monopolist

*A monopolist with a demand function $Q = 120 - P$ and total cost $TC = 2Q^2$ faces a per-unit tax of \$12. By how much will the consumer price increase?*

*(A) \$3 (B) \$6 (C) 2% (D) 10%*

The answer is **(C)**, and it is worth working in full because it shows how little of a per-unit tax may reach the consumer.

Write demand the way the firm sees it, as price in terms of quantity: $P = 120 - Q$. Total revenue is then

$$TR = PQ = 120Q - Q^2 \qquad \Rightarrow \qquad MR = \frac{\Delta TR}{\Delta Q} = 120 - 2Q$$

Marginal revenue falls twice as fast as the demand curve, which is the price effect in algebra: each extra unit sold requires a price cut on everything already being sold.

From $TC = 2Q^2$, marginal cost is $MC = 4Q$. Before the tax, the monopolist produces where $MC = MR$:

$$120 - 2Q = 4Q \quad \Rightarrow \quad Q = 20, \qquad P = 120 - 20 = 100$$

A per-unit tax of \$12 adds \$12 to the cost of every unit, so marginal cost becomes $MC = 4Q + 12$:

$$120 - 2Q = 4Q + 12 \quad \Rightarrow \quad 6Q = 108 \quad \Rightarrow \quad Q = 18, \qquad P = 120 - 18 = 102$$

The consumer price rises from \$100 to \$102 — an increase of \$2, which is **2%**. The monopolist absorbs the rest of the \$12 in the form of a lower quantity and a smaller margin. The distractors \$3 and \$6 are there for students who assume the tax is split in some fixed proportion; the actual share passed on depends on the slopes of marginal revenue and marginal cost, which is what the algebra works out.

## A note on the diagram question

One further question shows the demand curve of a price-setting firm and asks at which of three labelled points a monopoly may find it optimal to produce; the answer key gives *points A or B only*. The figure did not survive into the extracted text, so the labelled points cannot be recovered and the reasoning cannot be reconstructed. Work it from the principle above: the monopolist's chosen quantity is the one where marginal cost meets marginal revenue, and marginal revenue lies below the price at every quantity because of the price effect.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Quantity effect** | One more unit is sold, increasing total revenue by the price at which the unit is sold |
| **Price effect** | To sell the last unit, the monopolist must cut the market price on all units sold, which decreases total revenue |
| **Market power** | The ability of a producer to influence the market price by her own actions |
| **Allocative efficiency** | The condition, violated by price makers, that the price of the last unit equals its marginal cost |

# 11.1 The Labour Market: Competition and Monopsony

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## Two structures on the buying side

The labour market is analysed with the same tools as any other market, with one change of perspective: the firm is now the buyer and the worker is the seller. Two structures matter, and they differ in how much power the buyer has.

1. The **perfectly competitive labour market**
2. **Monopsony**

Two measures do the work in both:

| Term | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **Marginal factor cost (MFC)** | What it costs the firm to employ one more unit of the factor |
| **Marginal revenue product (MRP)** | The revenue the firm gains from employing one more unit of the factor |

## The perfectly competitive labour market

In perfect competition the labour market sets a price — the wage — and that price is the marginal factor cost for the individual firm. A firm hiring one more worker pays the going wage and nothing more, so the wage *is* the cost of the extra unit.

The demand for labour in an individual firm is its marginal revenue product, and it slopes downward. Firms here are price-takers in the labour market, and they hire the quantity at which the marginal revenue product meets the marginal factor cost — the optimal output rule again, applied to an input instead of an output: keep hiring while the next worker brings in more than they cost.

## Monopsony

In a **monopsony** the firm is the only firm in a labour market. Being the only buyer, it controls the wage rather than accepting one.

It employs the quantity at which marginal factor cost equals demand, which is the marginal revenue product — the same rule as before. But the wage it pays is not read off that intersection. The wage is the point on the **supply** curve at the quantity employed: having chosen how many workers to hire, the monopsonist pays only what it takes to attract that many.

The consequence is that a monopsonist's wage sits below the marginal revenue product of the workers it employs, and below the wage a competitive labour market would have produced.

## Worked example: when higher wages can raise total surplus

The practice set builds the question carefully. In perfectly competitive markets the equilibrium wage gives the most efficient outcome, so imposing a minimum wage reduces total social surplus, and labour unions negotiating a wage above what the employer wants to offer are a cause of deadweight loss. *However, when the markets are not perfectly competitive, higher wages may be beneficial for the economy.* Which market imperfection makes higher wages most likely to raise total social surplus: monopoly, monopsony, monopolistic competition, Bertrand oligopoly or Cournot oligopoly?

The answer is **monopsony**. It is the only option on the list that is an imperfection in the *labour* market; the other four describe a firm's power over the market for its product, which leaves the wage-setting story untouched.

The mechanism is the one described above. The monopsonist holds employment below the level a competitive market would reach, and pays a wage below the workers' marginal revenue product, because every extra worker it hires pushes the wage up along the supply curve. Fix the wage by law or by union agreement and that calculation disappears: the firm now faces a marginal factor cost equal to the fixed wage, exactly as a firm in a competitive labour market does, and it hires where the marginal revenue product meets it. A wage set above the monopsony wage can therefore raise employment as well as pay, and raise total surplus with it — the opposite of what the same policy does in a competitive labour market.

## Worked example: a lower wage and the substitution effect

*Catherine has just lost her job and found a new one right away, but at a lower wage rate. Based on the neoclassical theory of labour supply, the substitution effect of the lower wage will lead her to: (A) work fewer hours than before (B) work more hours than before (C) work the same hours as before (D) exit the labour market and thus supply zero hours of work*

The answer is **(A)**. The wage is the price of an hour of leisure, since an hour not worked is an hour of pay given up. When the wage falls, leisure becomes cheaper in exactly the sense the law of demand uses, and the **substitution effect** moves Catherine towards the thing that has become cheaper — more leisure, fewer hours of work.

## Worked example: derived demand

*The concept of derived demand is described by which of the following? (A) A decrease in the demand for theatre tickets will decrease the demand for actresses and actors. (B) If the salaries of basketball players increase, the quantity of basketball players demanded will decrease. (C) An increase in the income of consumers will increase the demand for opera tickets. (D) An increase in the demand for movie tickets will decrease the demand for video rentals. (E) A decrease in the price of movie tickets will increase the demand for movie tickets.*

The answer is **(A)**. **Derived demand** is the principle that demand for a factor of production comes from the demand for what it produces — which is precisely what the marginal revenue product says, since the revenue a worker generates depends on what the firm's output sells for. If audiences stop buying theatre tickets, the revenue an actor brings in falls, and the demand for actors falls with it.

The distractors are each a different idea in disguise: (B) is a movement along the demand curve for labour, (C) is an income effect, (D) is a relationship between substitute goods, and (E) is a movement along a demand curve for the good itself.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Marginal factor cost (MFC)** | The cost to the firm of employing one more unit of a factor; in a perfectly competitive labour market it equals the market wage |
| **Marginal revenue product (MRP)** | The revenue gained from employing one more unit of a factor; it is the individual firm's demand for labour and slopes downward |
| **Monopsony** | A labour market in which the firm is the only firm, and so controls the wage |
| **Derived demand** | Demand for a factor of production that comes from the demand for the good it produces |
| **Substitution effect (labour supply)** | The response to a change in the wage that comes from the change in the price of leisure — a lower wage leads to fewer hours worked |
